Reading in Data

# gaslight
load(url("https://github.com/Reilly-ConceptsCognitionLab/reillylab_publicdata/blob/main/gaslight.rda?raw=true"))

# handling empty 'Gender' observations
gaslight$Gender[gaslight$Gender == ""] <- NA

# subset
gaslight_sub <- gaslight |>
    select(Gender, gd_adult_story) |>
    drop_na(Gender)

# lookup database
load(url("https://github.com/Reilly-ConceptsCognitionLab/reillylab_publicdata/blob/main/lookup_Jul25.rda?raw=true"))

# create subset to analyze
lookup_sub <- lookup_Jul25 |>
    select(word, emo_anxiety_rescale, emo_sadness_rescale, emo_anger_rescale, emo_guilt_rescale)

Hypothesis

I infer that participants that identify as female will, on average, use words higher in anxiety and sadness in their gaslighting stories compared to their male-identifying counterparts, who will, on average, use words higher in anger and guilt.

Processing Pipeline

# start with cleaning genie!
emma_genie <- function(input, text_col = NULL, replacements = T, omit_stops = T, lemmatize = T) {
  # load in necessary libraries for the cleaning genie function
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(stringr)
  library(stringi)
  
  # different input types
  if(is.character(input) & is.null(text_col)) {
    df <- data.frame(text = input, stringsAsFactors = F)
    text_col <- "text"
  } else if (is.data.frame(input)) {
    df <- input
    if (is.null(text_col)) stop(paste("Provide text_col when input is a dataframe."))
    } else {
      stop(paste("Input must be a character vector or a dataframe"))
    }

  # if the column specified by "wordcol" does not exist in "df", show an error message
  if (!text_col %in% names(df)) {
    stop(paste("Column", text_col, "not found in dataframe"))
  }
  
  # load contraction & stop word corpora
  load(url("https://github.com/Reilly-ConceptsCognitionLab/reillylab_publicdata/blob/main/Temple_stops25.rda?raw=true"))
  load(url("https://github.com/Reilly-ConceptsCognitionLab/reillylab_publicdata/blob/main/replacements_25.rda?raw=true"))
  
  # creates an ID column, selects text column from text_col, forces it into a character, fixes any encoding issues, converts it to UTF-8, and changes all text to lowercase
  prep <- df |>
    mutate(
      ID = factor(seq_len(nrow(df))),
      
      initial_split = tryCatch(
        stri_enc_toutf8(
          as.character(.data[[text_col]]),
          is_unknown_8bit = T,
          validate = T
          ),
        error = function(e) {
          stri_encode(
            as.character(.data[[text_col]]), 
            to = "UTF-8"
            )
          }
        ) |> tolower()
      )
 
  # preserve NA values and standardize apostrophes to the ASCII apostrophe to ensure that code doesn't break further down the pipeline because of variance in apostrophe types
   prep <- prep |>
    mutate(
      initial_split = ifelse(
      is.na(initial_split), 
      NA_character_, 
      stri_replace_all_regex(initial_split, "[\u2018\u2019\u02BC\u201B\uFF07\u0092\u0091\u0060\u00B4\u2032\u2035]", "'")
      )
    )
   
   # splits text into individual tokens by word and puts them in row format, converts blank tokens to NA, removes the original text column (in left to right format)
   prep <- prep |>
     separate_rows(initial_split, sep = "[[:space:]]+") |>
     
     mutate(
       initial_split = ifelse(
       is.na(initial_split) | stri_isempty(initial_split), 
       NA_character_, 
       initial_split)
       ) |>
     
     select(-all_of(text_col))
   
   # PIECE OF GENIE THAT WILL BE EDITED BASED ON CLEANING NEEDS
   # removes punctuation, special characters, and whitespace. keeps apostrophes for contraction expansion purposes and hyphenated words to preserve their meaning.
   prep <- prep |>
     mutate(
       clean = initial_split,
       
       clean = ifelse(
         is.na(clean), 
         NA_character_, 
         stri_replace_all_regex(clean, "[^a-zA-Z0-9-']", "") 
         ),
       
       clean = ifelse(
         is.na(clean), 
         NA_character_, 
         str_squish(clean)
         ),
       
       clean = ifelse(
         is.na(clean), 
         NA_character_, 
         stri_replace_all_regex(clean, "[^a-z'-]", "")
         )
       )
   
   # expands contractions with keeping all other words and preserving NAs
   if(replacements) {
     map <- setNames(
       tolower(replacements_25$replacement),
       tolower(replacements_25$word)
     )
     
     prep <- prep |>
       mutate(
         is_replacement = ifelse(
           is.na(clean),
           NA_character_,
           dplyr::recode(tolower(clean), !!!map, .default = clean)
         )
       ) |>
       select(-is_replacement)
   }
   
   # splits new clean version into tokens and forces individual words into rows; removes all apostrophes
   prep <- prep |>
     separate_rows(clean, sep = "[[:space:]]+", convert = T) |>
     mutate(
       clean = ifelse(
         is.na(clean) | stri_isempty(clean),
         NA_character_,
         stri_replace_all_regex(clean, "'", "")
       ),
       ID_post_split = seq_len(dplyr::n())
     )
   
   # lemmatizes words (basic dictionary form)
   if(lemmatize) {
     prep <- prep |>
       mutate(
         clean = ifelse(
           is.na(clean),
           NA_character_,
           textstem::lemmatize_strings(clean)
         )
       )
   }
   
   # removes stop words and flags where they were with NAs
   if (omit_stops) {
     stopwords <- tolower(Temple_stops25$word)
     
     prep <- prep |>
       mutate(
         is_stopword = ifelse(
           is.na(clean),
           NA,
           clean %in% stopwords
         ),
         clean = ifelse(
           is_stopword,
           NA_character_,
           clean
         )
       ) |>
       select(-is_stopword)
   }
   
   return(prep)
}

# clean gaslighting text
clean <- emma_genie(gaslight_sub, text_col = "gd_adult_story")

# join the lookup subset with the cleaned gaslighting text
combined <- clean |>
  left_join(lookup_sub, by = c("clean" = "word")) |>
  mutate(Gender = as.factor(Gender))

# create averages for each of the emotion variables grouped by ID number
combined <- combined |>
  group_by(ID) |>
  mutate(anger_avg = mean(emo_anger_rescale, na.rm = T),
         guilt_avg = mean(emo_guilt_rescale, na.rm = T),
         sad_avg = mean(emo_sadness_rescale, na.rm = T),
         anxiety_avg = mean(emo_anxiety_rescale, na.rm= T))

# relevel factors (done post-hoc; better for interpretability)
combined$Gender <- relevel(combined$Gender, ref = "Male")

Justification

I used the cleaning genie to perform text cleaning, splitting, and tokenizing, as I am interested in looking at individual words and their associations as well as general, larger picture questions. By putting each individual word, in its most basic and dictionary-level form, in a row, I’m able to zoom out by data wrangling post-hoc, and zoom in on the already split, unlisted, tokenized, and lemmatized words.

I opted to look exclusively at the story data due to the conversational and creation aspects of it. When it comes to emotional language, this data will be much more interesting than the definitions.

I chose anger, anxiety, guilt, and sadness because they are words that may be elicited by a gaslighting experience, and are also negatively valenced. I find that I’m always more interested in how negatively a person feels; occupational hazard, I suppose.

I created averages of each emotion chosen so that I could get a zoomed out picture before diving into (spoiler!) exploratory analyses. I find that it’s always better to make the zoomed-out association before zooming back in, and my hypothesis allows that to happen.

Exploratory Analyses!

Hypothesis

Screw it, I’m doing some exploratory analyses! I can see that women-identifying participants are, on average, using more negatively valenced words in general when telling their stories. I’m interested in whether that trend is moderated by “time”, in that there will be differences in gender identity on when–in the story–valenced words are used.

Data Prep

# creating 'time' variable (essentially word count, but to serve as a time
# anchor for each participant)
combined_explor <- combined |>
    group_by(ID) |>
    mutate(time = row_number(), time_c = scale(time, scale = F), word_count = n()) |>
    ungroup()

Statistics

exp_anger <- lmer(emo_anger_rescale ~ Gender * time_c + word_count + (1 | ID), data = combined_explor)  # controlling for word count
summary(exp_anger)

Written Report

Overall, there seems to be a gender difference in the averaged usage of select negatively valenced emotion words in a story on gaslighting, where women, on average, use words higher in anger (b = 0.005, SE = 0.001, t = 3.459, p < 0.001), higher in guilt (b = 0.004, SE = 0.001, t = 2.87, p = 0.004), higher in anxiety (b = 0.027, SE = 0.001, t = 23.38, p < 0.001), and higher in sadness (b = 0.019, SE = 0.001, t = 15.88, p < 0.001). While this does not fully match the original hypothesis, it does confirm half (women do, on average, use words that are considered anxious and sad). These results that women will, on average, use more negatively valenced words than men when describing a story with themes of gaslighting.

As for the exploratory results, we do not see a significant interaction effect between gender and time, suggesting that the trajectory of negatively valenced emotions over the time of telling a gaslighting story does not significantly differ by gender (anger: b < 0.001, SE < 0.001, t = 0.386, p = 0.6995; guilt: b < 0.001, SE < 0.001, t = 1.338, p = 0.1810; anxiety: b < 0.001, SE < 0.001, t = 0.589, p = 0.5557; sadness: b < 0.001, SE < 0.001, t = 0.125, p = 0.9002). These results do not support the exploratory hypothesis that time moderated the established relationships between gender and the selected negatively valenced emotions, and suggest that there may be additional underlying linguistic components that could further parse out the relationship between gender and negative valence word usage. I would be interested to see if this would hold for all of the negative emotions in the Lookup database, and I would also like to see if concreteness or semantic visualization may explain more of why women seem to use more negatively valenced emotion words.
